{{Short description|Graph modeling collaboration in a social network}}
In [[mathematics]] and [[social science]], a '''collaboration graph'''<ref>{{cite journal|last=Odda|first=Tom|year=1979|title=On properties of a well-known graph or what is your Ramsey number? Topics in graph theory.|journal=Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences|publisher=[[New York Academy of Sciences]]|location=[[New York City|New York]], 1977|volume=328|pages=166–172|doi=10.1111/j.1749-6632.1979.tb17777.x|s2cid=84887029 }}</ref><ref>Frank Harary. ''Topics in Graph Theory''.  [[New York Academy of Sciences]], 1979. {{ISBN|0-89766-028-5}}</ref> is a graph modeling some [[social network]] where the vertices represent participants of that network (usually individual people) and where two distinct participants are joined by an edge whenever there is a collaborative relationship between them of a particular kind. Collaboration graphs are used to measure the closeness of collaborative relationships between the participants of the network.

==Types considered in the literature==
The most well-studied collaboration graphs include:
*Collaboration graph of mathematicians also known as the [[Erdős number|'''Erdős collaboration graph''']],<ref>{{cite journal | url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/S0378-8733(00)00023-X | doi=10.1016/S0378-8733(00)00023-X | title=Some analyses of Erdős collaboration graph | date=2000 | last1=Batagelj | first1=Vladimir | last2=Mrvar | first2=Andrej | journal=Social Networks | volume=22 | issue=2 | pages=173–186 | url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>Casper Goffman. ''And what is your Erdos number?'', [[American Mathematical Monthly]], vol. 76 (1979), p. 791</ref> where two mathematicians are joined by an edge whenever they co-authored a paper together (with possibly other co-authors present).
*Collaboration graph of movie actors, also known as the '''Hollywood graph''' or [[co-stardom network]],<ref>Chaomei Chen, C. Chen. ''Mapping Scientific Frontiers: The Quest for Knowledge Visualization.'' [[Springer-Verlag]] New York. January 2003. {{ISBN|978-1-85233-494-9}}.  See p. 94.</ref><ref>Fan Chung, Linyuan Lu. ''Complex Graphs and Networks, Vol. 107.'' [[American Mathematical Society]]. October 2006. {{ISBN|978-0-8218-3657-6}}. See p. 16</ref><ref>Albert-László Barabási and Réka Albert, [http://www.sciencemag.org/cgi/content/abstract/286/5439/509 "Emergence of scaling in random networks".] ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]'', vol. 286 (1999), no. 5439, pp. 509–512</ref> where two movie actors are joined by an edge whenever they appeared in a movie together.
*Collaborations graphs in other social networks, such as sports, including the "NBA graph" whose vertices are players where two players are joined by an edge if they have ever played together on the same team.<ref>V. Boginski, S. Butenko, P.M. Pardalos, O. Prokopyev. ''Collaboration networks in sports''. pp. 265–277. Economics, Management, and Optimization in Sports. [[Springer-Verlag]], New York, February 2004. {{ISBN|978-3-540-20712-2}}</ref>
*Co-authorship graphs in published articles, where individual nodes may be assigned either at the level of the author, institution, or country. These types of graphs are useful in establishing and evaluating research networks.<ref>{{cite journal | author = Malbas, Vincent Schubert | year = 2015 | title = Mapping the collaboration networks of biomedical research in Southeast Asia | journal = PeerJ PrePrints | volume = 3 | pages = e1160 | doi = 10.7287/peerj.preprints.936v1 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

==Features==
By construction, the collaboration graph is a [[simple graph]], since it has no loop-edges and no multiple edges.
The collaboration graph need not be connected. Thus each person who never co-authored a joint paper represents an isolated vertex in the collaboration graph of mathematicians.

Both the collaboration graph of mathematicians and movie actors were shown to have "small world topology": they have a very large number of vertices, most of small degree, that are highly clustered, and a "giant" connected  component with small average distances between vertices.<ref>Jerrold W. Grossman. ''The evolution of the mathematical research collaboration graph.'' Proceedings of the Thirty-Third Southeastern International Conference on Combinatorics, Graph Theory and Computing ([[Boca Raton, FL]], 2002). Congressus Numerantium. Vol. 158 (2002), pp. 201–212.</ref>

==Collaboration distance==
The distance between two people/nodes in a collaboration graph is called the '''collaboration distance'''.<ref>{{Cite book|first2=Michel-Marie|last2=Deza|author2-link=Michel Deza|first1=Elena|last1=Deza|author1-link=Elena Deza|title=Dictionary of Distances|publisher=Elsevier|year=2006|isbn=978-0-444-52087-6|chapter=Ch. 22|page=279}}.</ref> Thus the collaboration distance between two distinct nodes is equal to the smallest number of edges in an edge-path connecting them. If no path connecting two nodes in a collaboration graph exists, the collaboration distance between them is said to be infinite.

The collaboration distance may be used, for instance, for evaluating the citations of an author, a group of authors or a journal.<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Bras-Amorós, M. |author2=Domingo-Ferrer, J. |author3=Torra, V. | year = 2011 | title = A bibliometric index based on the collaboration distance between cited and citing authors | journal = Journal of Informetrics | volume = 5 | issue = 2 | pages = 248–264 | doi = 10.1016/j.joi.2010.11.001 |hdl=10261/138172 }}</ref>

In the collaboration graph of mathematicians, the collaboration distance from a particular person to [[Paul Erdős]] is called the [[Erdős number]] of that person. [[MathSciNet]] has a free online tool<ref>[https://www.ams.org/mathscinet/collaborationDistance.html MathSciNet Collaboration Distance Calculator.] [[American Mathematical Society]]. Accessed May 23, 2008</ref> for computing the collaboration distance between any two mathematicians as well as the Erdős number of a mathematician. This tool also shows the actual chain of co-authors that realizes the collaboration distance.

For the Hollywood graph, an analog of the Erdős number, called the [[Bacon number]], has also been considered, which measures the collaboration distance to [[Kevin Bacon]].

==Generalizations==
Some generalizations of the collaboration graph of mathematicians have also been considered. There is a [[hypergraph]] version, where individual mathematicians are vertices and where a group of mathematicians (not necessarily just two) constitutes a [[hyperedge]] if there is a paper of which they were all co-authors.<ref>Frank Harary. ''Topics in Graph Theory''. [[New York Academy of Sciences]], 1979. {{ISBN|0-89766-028-5}} See p. 166</ref>

A [[multigraph]] version of a collaboration graph has also been considered where two mathematicians are joined by <math>k</math> edges if they co-authored exactly <math>k</math> papers together. Another variation is a weighted collaboration graph where with rational weights where two mathematicians are joined by an edge with weight <math>\tfrac{1}{k}</math> whenever they co-authored exactly <math>k</math> papers together.<ref>Mark E.J. Newman. {{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20130203051202/http://www.springerlink.com/content/v8f1fxyltq0b9ejf/|title=''Who Is the Best Connected Scientist? A Study of Scientific Coauthorship Networks.''}}  Lecture Notes in Physics, vol. 650, pp. 337–370. [[Springer-Verlag]]. [[Berlin]]. 2004. {{ISBN|978-3-540-22354-2}}.</ref> This model naturally leads to the notion of a "rational Erdős number".<ref>Alexandru T. Balaban and Douglas J. Klein.{{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20120729100300/http://www.akademiai.com/content/k5712p44j772224t/|title=''Co-authorship, rational Erdős numbers, and resistance distances in graphs.''}} [[Scientometrics]], vol. 55 (2002), no. 1, pp. 59–70.</ref>
